title: Following Jesus: Discipleship
lead: In the Gospels a disciple (mathētēs, "learner") is someone who leaves home and work to follow a teacher on the road, as Elisha followed Elijah and as students followed Jewish teachers; Jesus asks for more than a teacher did: to follow him to a cross. The Old Testament roots, the Gospel sayings on the cost of following, and how the churches have lived them are gathered here.

sections.b: The pattern of a master and a follower runs through the Old Testament: Joshua served Moses (Exodus 24:13; Numbers 11:28), Elisha left his plowing to go after Elijah and wait on him (1 Kings 19:19–21), and Ruth vowed to go wherever Naomi went (Ruth 1:16–17). In Jesus' time pupils followed their teachers and served them; later rabbinic texts list a disciple's duties to his master (Mishnah Avot 1:4; Babylonian Talmud, Ketubot 96a). What set Jesus apart was that he called people himself, often abruptly, and called them to follow him, not the Torah or a school. Martin Hengel argued that this makes Jesus more like a charismatic prophet than a rabbi.
